entries.note: First Dutch [[from:New Amsterdam]], renamed in 1664 after the [[from:Duke of York]], not directly after the city of [[see:York]].
The Dutch settlement's name, after Amsterdam, which grew from [[see:Fort Amsterdam]] and became [[gave:New York]] under English control.
Dutch fort and trading post on Manhattan Island, founded around 1624, where [[see:New Amsterdam]] began.
Discussed often in earlier episodes of the podcast.
Discussed often in earlier episodes of the podcast.
The future James II, granted the land by his brother [[see:Charles II]]; [[gave:New York]] is named after him, and his title after [[from:York]].
Developed from Roman [[from:Eboracum]] through Anglo-Saxon [[from:Eoforwic]] and Viking [[from:Jorvik]], then worn down by Norman accents and centuries of use.
The Roman name for [[gave:York]], the oldest known, probably adapted from an earlier Celtic name.
Anglo-Saxon reshaping of [[from:Eboracum]] using eofor, wild boar, from a misunderstanding of the Roman name's sound; it became Viking [[gave:Jorvik]].
Norse version of [[from:Eoforwic]], used when the Vikings made the city their capital; it later became [[gave:York]].
Adjective meaning relating to New York, containing [[from:Eboracum]] and the demonym ending [[from:-ensian]].
A demonym ending, seen in [[see:Novaboracensian]] and [[see:Leodensian]].
A word for people from a place, discussed in an earlier episode.
Loosely named after its river, although the river is called the Aire; Rob calls the full story long and not very interesting.
The word for a person from [[see:Leeds]], with the [[see:-ensian]] ending.
Nickname for New York from [[see:Washington Irving]], after an English village said to feign madness, locally Goatum, goat hamlet; it inspired Batman's city.
Writer of Dutch-flavoured New York satire who first called the city [[see:Gotham]], in his periodical [[see:Salmagundi]].
[[see:Washington Irving]]'s satirical periodical, where New York was first called [[see:Gotham]].

entries.term: Merry Tales of the Mad Men of Gotham
entries.note: A Middle English collection of stories about a town whose people pretend to be idiots, the source of the nickname [[see:Gotham]].
In the story, the people of [[see:Gotham]] acted mad so he would build his hunting lodge somewhere else.
Co-creator of Batman with Bob Kane, who gave Batman's city the name [[see:Gotham]].
A French rendering, recorded by [[see:Robert de La Salle]], of Miami-Illinois [[from:shikaakwa]], meaning garlic, after the wild garlic in the area.
French explorer mapping routes for New France who recorded the name that became [[see:Chicago]] in the 1600s.
Nickname for [[see:Chicago]] that began in sports and civic rivalries with Cincinnati, describing boastful windbags rather than the weather.
An insult from [[from:A. J. Liebling]]'s 1952 essays portraying [[see:Chicago]] as inferior to New York, which the city adopted for an improv troupe.
New Yorker journalist and critic whose essays on Chicago gave rise to the nickname [[see:Second City]].
A later Chicago slogan answering the insult [[see:Second City]].
New York's nickname, first a jibe about the city taking nutrients from other apples, then adopted by locals, like [[see:Second City]]; also has horse-racing origins discussed earlier.
From western Great Lakes Indigenous languages, often explained as good land, good place or gathering place; it's unclear which language or word it came from.
One of the few cities named after a specific Native American person, [[from:Chief Seattle]].
A 19th-century Native American leader, important in relations with settlers, after whom [[gave:Seattle]] is named.
Shares its Muscogee Creek source, talahasi, town or old settlement, with [[same-root:Tallahassee]]; Creek families carried the name west after the [[see:Trail of Tears]].
From Muscogee Creek talahasi, meaning town or old settlement, the same source as [[same-root:Tulsa]].
The forced removal after which Creek families from [[see:Tallahassee]] resettled in Indian Territory, bringing the name that became [[see:Tulsa]].
The fortified town of St Peter, named after an abbey; one of the names with the Anglo-Saxon element [[from:burh]].
A tiny Welsh city with an obvious namesake, St David.
Probably the most obvious American city named after a person.
Named after [[from:Philippe II, Duke of Orléans]], whose title comes from a place; like [[see:New York]].
Regent of France for Louis XV, after whom [[gave:New Orleans]] is named.
Columbus, Ohio, was named long after Columbus, because an Ohio lawmaker who admired him persuaded others; compare [[see:District of Columbia]].
One of the best-known places named after Columbus, like [[see:Columbus]], Ohio.
Named after [[from:Sam Houston]].
The namesake of [[gave:Houston]].
Its namesake has been forgotten; one theory says it was [[from?:George M. Dallas]].
Served under President James K. Polk; one theory says he is the namesake of [[gave?:Dallas]].
Named after [[from:Andrew Jackson]].
The namesake of [[gave:Jacksonville]].
Named after [[from:William J. Worth]].
Senior officer commanding US forces in Texas, after whom [[gave:Fort Worth]] is named.
One of the few cities named after a woman, [[from:Charlotte of Mecklenburg-Strelitz]]; incorporated in 1768 while North Carolina was a British colony.
Wife of King George III and the namesake of [[gave:Charlotte]].
Named after [[from:James W. Denver]].
The namesake of [[gave:Denver]].
Named after [[from:Francis Nash]].
The namesake of [[gave:Nashville]].
The name of both an English and an American city, meaning settlement of the people of [[from:Beorma]], from [[from:-ing (noun suffix)]] and [[from:-ham]].
The person hidden in the name [[gave:Birmingham]].
In place names it means the people of the person named before it, as in [[see:Birmingham]] and [[see:Nottingham]].
One of many suffixes broadly meaning settlement, homestead or farmstead, as in [[see:Birmingham]] and [[see:Southampton]].
Called [[from:Snottingham]] until fairly recently, meaning settlement of the people of [[from:Snot]], a fact enjoyed in rival Derby.
The long-standing earlier name of [[gave:Nottingham]], settlement of the people of [[from:Snot]].
The person whose people gave their name to [[gave:Snottingham]].
The only English city named after a woman, probably [[from:Wulfrun]]; originally Wulfrun's high town, its -hampton differs from the usual [[see:-ham]] plus town.
A woman granted land by [[see:Æthelred the Unready]], thought to be the namesake of [[gave:Wolverhampton]]; the hosts think her name should come back.
The king who granted [[see:Wulfrun]] the land that became [[see:Wolverhampton]].
The Texas capital was first called [[from:Waterloo]], then renamed for [[from:Stephen F. Austin]].
The original name of [[gave:Austin]], chosen in 1839, perhaps after the battle; the European Waterloo means watery clearing or wet forest.
Leader of the first major Anglo-American settlement of Mexican Texas, sometimes called the father of Texas, after whom [[gave:Austin]] was renamed.
In a local joke, the Texas vice president, whose middle name was Bonaparte, pushed to rename [[see:Waterloo]].
London railway terminus where trains from France used to arrive, which the hosts find tactless given the name [[see:Waterloo]].
No one knows its origin; it comes from [[from:Londinium]], based on some Celtic or even pre-Celtic name, and it may be England's oldest city name.
The earliest known form of [[gave:London]], based on an unknown Celtic name; [[from?:Lindon]] has been proposed.
A proposed Celtic source for [[gave?:Londinium]], combining [[from:lin]] and [[from:dun]], though no one knows for sure.
A Celtic word for pool, found in [[see:Dublin]], [[see:Lindon]] and [[see:Lindum Colonia]].
A Celtic element meaning hill or hill fort, as in [[see:Dundee]], [[see:Lindon]] and [[see:Din Eidyn]].
Means black pool, containing the Celtic [[from:lin]].
Means hill fort on the River Tay, with [[from:dun]].
Formerly [[from:Losantiville]], renamed after the [[from:Society of the Cincinnati]], ultimately from [[from:Cincinnatus]], whose name means curly-haired: the curly hair city.
The first name of [[gave:Cincinnati]].
A Revolutionary War officers' organisation founded in 1783 and named after [[from:Cincinnatus]]; [[gave:Cincinnati]] was renamed in its honour.
Roman hero who left farming to save the city in days; his name comes from cincinnus, curly hair, and gave [[gave:Cincinnati]] its name.
A contraction of Roman [[from:Lindum Colonia]], from a Celtic name with [[from:lin]], pool; the surname, and Abraham Lincoln, ultimately link back to it.
Roman name of [[gave:Lincoln]], joining a Celtic name containing [[from:lin]] with [[from:colonia]].
The second part of [[see:Lindum Colonia]], described somewhat confusedly as a military depot for centurions.
After a red-painted boundary pole seen by [[see:Pierre Le Moyne d'Iberville]], probably translating the Choctaw [[from:Istrouma]].
French explorer who saw the red pole that named [[see:Baton Rouge]] while travelling up the Mississippi in the late 17th century.
Name for the site recorded by a carpenter in 1723, marking a boundary between two tribes; the source of [[gave:Baton Rouge]].
The Anglo-Saxon word for a fortified town, appearing in place names as burgh, bury and borough: [[see:Peterborough]], [[see:Edinburgh]], [[see:Bury]].
A place named simply from [[from:burh]], a former Anglo-Saxon fortified town.
Also -caster or -cester, meaning Roman fort, from Latin castrum; the Anglo-Saxons added it to mark former Roman forts.
An example of a city name with [[from:-chester]].
An example of a hard-to-pronounce name whose -cester is [[from:-chester]].
The place that embodies [[from:-chester]], meaning Roman fort.
Rob's favourite; the Roman fort ([[from:-chester]]) at the breast-shaped hill, distantly related to [[same-root?:mammary]] and perhaps [[same-root?:mother]].
Very distantly related to the man- of [[same-root:Manchester]].
Perhaps very distantly related to the man- of [[same-root?:Manchester]].
Named after a local Celtic tribe plus [[from:-chester]]; the Anglo-Saxon form contracted over time to Leicester, hence the odd spelling.
Originally [[from:Grantabridge]]; reportedly the Normans couldn't say Granta, so the city and the river became [[see:Cam]].
The Anglo-Saxon word, brycg, has barely changed in over a thousand years; it's the -bridge of [[see:Cambridge]].
The original name of [[gave:Cambridge]], after the River [[from:Granta]].
The river's old name, which gave [[gave:Grantabridge]] and which Normans supposedly couldn't pronounce.
The river's current name, which it shares with [[see:Cambridge]].
Means the [[from:ford]] where oxen crossed, maybe the most boring city name of all.
A river crossing shallow enough to walk through, as in [[see:Oxford]] and [[see:Hereford]].
The [[from:ford]] where an army crossed, from Old English [[from:here]].
Lost Old English word for an army, replaced by French [[see:army]]; preserved in [[see:Hereford]].
The French word that replaced Old English [[see:here]].
Another Anglo-Saxon word for a settlement, as in [[see:Norwich]].
Means northern [[from:wick]], a city in [[see:East Anglia]].
A region still named after the Angles who lived there; home of [[see:Norwich]].
The precursor of [[gave:town]], as in [[see:Norton]], [[see:Sutton]], [[see:Southampton]] and [[see:Boston]].
Descends from the place-name ending [[from:-ton]].
Every Norton is the north [[from:-ton]], or north town.
The south town, from [[from:-ton]]; the surname Sutton means south town.
A muddle of south, [[from:-ham]] (settlement) and [[from:-ton]] (town).
The US city is named after Boston, Lincolnshire, Isaac Johnson's hometown, which means [[from:St Botolph]]'s town; earlier names were Algonquian and [[see:Trimountaine]].
A seventh-century East Anglian saint of travel and protection whose town became [[gave:Boston]].
A French-derived name used by early Puritan settlers for [[see:Boston]]'s hilly peninsula, still carried by [[gave:Tremont Street]].
A Boston street that still carries the name [[from:Trimountaine]].
Short for [[from:El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles]]; its English pronunciation has varied, with British speakers favouring a more Greek-Latin spelling pronunciation.

entries.term: the town of our lady the queen of the angels
entries.original: El Pueblo de Nuestra Señora la Reina de los Ángeles
entries.translation: the town of our lady the queen of the angels
entries.note: Full name given by the 44 settlers called the Pobladores in the 1700s; longer versions add 'of the Porciúncula River'; the source of [[gave:Los Angeles]].
Means the meadows, fertile watered lowlands in arid terrain; the hosts discuss whether to say 'Las' or 'Lass', as in [[see:Viva Las Vegas]].
The song quoted to show how [[see:Las Vegas]] is commonly pronounced.
Named after St Francis, one of the US cities named after saints.
From San Diego de Alcalá, the saint Didacus of Alcalá.
The Welsh capital: [[from:caer]], fort, plus a Welsh form of [[see:Taff]], meaning fort on the River Taff.
Means fort, seen in [[see:Cardiff]] and the English city [[see:Carlisle]].
An English city whose name also contains [[from:caer]], fort.
The English name of the river whose Welsh form forms the second part of [[see:Cardiff]].
A common Welsh place-name prefix meaning river mouth, as in [[see:Aberystwyth]].
Mystical-sounding and hard to spell, but it just means the mouth ([[from:aber]]) of the River Ystwyth.
Means church, as in [[see:Llanfairpwllgwyngyll]] and [[see:Llandudno]].
The very long Welsh place name, which begins with [[from:llan]] and refers to the church of St Mary.
Means the church ([[from:llan]]) of St Tudno.
Means valley, as in [[see:Cwmbran]].
The Welsh name for Wales, a Brittonic self-designation; the same word as [[same-root:Cumbria]] and [[same-root:Cambria]].
Related to [[same-root:Cymru]].
Another rendering of the same word as [[same-root:Cymru]].
A Welsh town thought to mean valley ([[from:cwm]]) of the crow.
Nothing to do with swans or the sea: an Old Norse name meaning Sveinn's island, with the suffix [[from:ey]].
Means island; a common suffix in places where the Vikings stopped, as in [[see:Swansea]].
Welsh football club in which Snoop Dogg and Martha Stewart have bought minority stakes.
An Anglo-Saxon name with [[from:-ham]], meaning Wryhtel's settlement; its football club is owned by Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.
A Celtic–Anglo-Saxon hybrid: [[from:burh]] plus a Brittonic Edin-, possibly Welsh [[from?:eithin]], gorse; once called [[from:Din Eidyn]].
Welsh for gorse, a rough bush, similar to the probable source of the Edin- in [[gave?:Edinburgh]].
The area's earlier name, with Din a form of [[from:dun]]; it gave [[gave:Edinburgh]] and was echoed in New Zealand's [[gave:Dunedin]].
New Zealand city known for rugby, another rendering of the old name for Edinburgh, [[from:Din Eidyn]].
From Scottish Gaelic Glaschu, green glen, with [[from:glas]]; similar in meaning to [[see:Edinburgh]].
A Celtic colour word for green, blue or pale watery shades, discussed in an earlier colour-names episode; it's in [[see:Glasgow]].
Suggested in the 1860s by [[see:Jack Swilling]]'s group, after the mythical bird reborn from destruction, since the city was built on abandoned [[see:Hohokam]] canals.
A Civil War veteran who helped build the new city on old canals, and whose group suggested the name [[see:Phoenix (city)]].
Indigenous culture that built hundreds of miles of Salt River Valley canals, whose abandoned remains inspired the name [[see:Phoenix (city)]].
